title_original: UK’s Sky restructures its pay-1 acquisitions team as film execs depart
excerpt_original: EXCLUSIVE: Changes have unsettled the wider UK film industry, which has seen pay-TV firms retreat from pay-1 deals.

blocks.text: Source: (c) Crossbow Films Limited 2023
Claes Bang as William Tell
EXCLUSIVE: UK broadcaster Sky has restructured its acquisitions team, with four executives leaving, including staff responsible for buying pay-TV rights to studio and independent feature films.

The changes have unsettled the wider UK film industry, which has seen pay-TV firms retreat from pay-1 deals in recent years, although Sky insists it remains committed to its film slate and strong relationships with its distribution partners.

links.text: pay-TV firms retreat from pay-1 deals

blocks.text: The changes follow a restructure of Andrew Orr’s separate Sky Original film team last year , which was cut from seven to three executives. Orr’s Sky Originals film team has a different focus to the acquisitions team, with the former taking all rights to 10-15 films per year while the latter takes pay-TV rights only.

links.text: separate Sky Original film team last year

blocks.text: The latest developments see Benedicte Steinsrud poised to leave her role as head of acquisitions focused on Sky Cinema and transactional platform Sky Store. Steinsrud joined Sky in 2024 from Nordic streamer Viaplay, and is relocating to be closer to her family.

Three other executives are also leaving the acquisitions team, understood to include one responsible for sourcing independent feature films from UK distributors and another for acquiring independent series. An internal-focused executive from the acquisitions team is also leaving.

Sky said their responsibilities will be split across the remaining acquisitions team, which continues to be led by group director of acquisitions Katie Keenan, with Lucy Criddle, director of acquisitions and strategic projects, reporting into her. Between them, they lead Sky’s acquisition strategy across film, TV drama and entertainment.

The company said that Rachel McCartney’s current role as acquisitions manager will become focused on film, working alongside the senior acquisitions leadership overseeing key content supplier relationships across genres, including the US studios.

Under the new structure, Facundo Bailez has taken on the role of head of acquisitions and editorial, working with Sky acquisition managers to shape and develop the content pipeline. Hadi Leclercq will take on a head of commercial role within the team.
Sky insisted there would be no change to its acquisitions strategy or direction across any genre, including film, as a result of the changes.
Industry concern

However, within the UK film industry, there is concern a smaller Sky team will lack enough resource to be able to be as responsive in terms of acquisitions, particularly at a time when distributors find it harder than ever to secure vital pay-1 deals for their films .

links.text: find it harder than ever to secure vital pay-1 deals for their films

blocks.text: Sky remains an important business partner to many UK independent distributors, although it has cut back on its pay-1 film launches in recent years, as have other streamers and pay-TV firms.
It is understood Sky currently buys around 40-50 films from independent UK distributors a year to top up its output from US studios and mini-majors.

Recent acquisitions from UK independent distributors include William Tell and Pets On A Train from Altitude, The Toxic Avenger and Beast Of War from Signature, Prisoner Of War from Kaleidescope, Grand Prix Of Europe from Kazoo, and Tom & Jerry Forbidden Compass and Looney Tunes: The Day the Earth Blew Up from Vertigo Releasing.

The changes also come against a background of wider cuts at Comcast-owned Sky. Earlier this year Sky restructured its entertainment commissioning team. In 2025, Sky announced it would stop commissioning all new original children’s programming and in 2024 revealed 1,000 job cuts. Sky is expected to close its acquisition of UK broadcaster ITV soon, which is likely to lead to further restructuring.
Film strategy

In recent years, Sky has cut back on premiering feature films – moving from a strategy of launching a new film every night to premiering three new titles a week on consecutive weekend nights over Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays.

Many of these film launches come from studio partners. However, Sky’s once firm grip on pay-1 rights to prized US studio movies has weakened considerably in recent years due to competition from streamers such as Netflix and Amazon as well as the launch of US studio platforms such as HBO Max and Paramount+.
In January, Sony agreed a global pay-1 licensing deal with Netflix, which will replace Sky’s deal, depriving the pay-TV firm of a key source of Hollywood movies.

Sky has non-exclusive output deals with Paramount, which also premieres its titles on Paramount+, and with Warner Bros, which also launches its films on HBO Max. Following the merger between Paramount and Warner Bros, these deals may be renegotiated in the future so that the studios premiere their titles on a combined platform.

That leaves Comcast-owned Sky’s sister company Universal as its only exclusive pay-1 studio partner. Sky used to have a pay-1 output deal with leading UK distributor Entertainment Film, but the majority of its titles, such as Marty Supreme, are now acquired by Amazon for pay-1.
It is thought Sky might seek to make up for the loss of its Sony deal by acquiring more content from mini-majors such as Lionsgate and Studiocanal.
Another possibility – which would be good news for the UK sector – is Sky buys more from the independent sector to compensate for a lack of studio films.
